research_question: What do published AI accelerator bandwidth figures establish, what do they not establish, and under which documented conditions can two of them be compared?

scope.technical: Memory, GPU-to-GPU fabric, host-link and scale-out bandwidth figures for AMD MI300X and NVIDIA Rubin, with the HBM4 stack and CXL/PCIe figures used by reference pathway B
scope.temporal: Sources dated 2022 to 2026-11-05; figures as recorded in releases 001 and 004 and the conflict register, with the IDE-009 reconciliations
excluded: Measured application or collective throughput, which no reviewed source publishes
Any statement that one product is faster or better

boundary: A research candidate on metric compatibility, not an assessment of products. A comparability class says whether two published figures measure the same thing on documented terms; it never says which product is better. It records no human or scientific review and does not promote any Atlas relationship.

comparability_classes.comparable_on_documented_terms: Same hierarchy level, unit dimension, direction convention and status, all stated by the sources
comparability_classes.conditionally_comparable: Comparable only after a stated rule-based normalization or with stated conditions attached to every use
comparability_classes.not_comparable: The figures measure different things: different hierarchy level, aggregation scope or metric
comparability_classes.indeterminate: A descriptor needed to decide (direction, scope or counting convention) is not stated

normalization_rules.description: Convert a bit rate to bytes by dividing by eight. Line encoding and protocol overhead are not removed.
Halve a figure to a per-direction value. Assumes the two directions are equal.
Divide a stated aggregate evenly by a stated member count. Gives arithmetic consistency only, never a per-member figure the publisher states.
Multiply a stated per-link figure by a stated link count in the same direction convention.

normalizations.note: Seven links at 128 GB/s sum to exactly 896 GB/s. Arithmetic; not a publisher statement; it is consistent with a per-GPU reading but does not establish it.
A fully connected eight-GPU system has 28 distinct links; at 128 GB/s that totals 3,584 GB/s. Arithmetic; not a publisher statement; it shows what a platform-wide sum would be under that topology.
130 TB/s over eight GPUs is 16.25 TB/s, matching neither 22 nor 19.2 TB/s. Arithmetic; not a publisher statement.
216 TB/s over 72 GPUs is 3 TB/s, the same as the page's GPU column. Arithmetic; not a publisher statement.
24 TB/s, marked bidirectional, over eight GPUs is 3 TB/s per GPU, while the same page's individual-GPU row gives 3.6 TB/s. Arithmetic; not a publisher statement.
3.6 TB/s stated bidirectional is 1.8 TB/s per direction if the directions are equal. Arithmetic; not a publisher statement.
1.6 Tb/s is 200 GB/s before encoding and protocol overhead. Arithmetic; not a publisher statement.

rejected_normalizations.why: NVIDIA does not state the direction of 3.0 TB/s, so treating it as bidirectional (or as per direction) to reconcile it with 3.6 TB/s is unsupported.
The scope of 896 GB/s is unresolved, so dividing it across eight GPUs, or treating it as already per GPU, assumes the answer to the open question.
The July article states 3,600 GB/s without a direction; the January article's 'bidirectional' cannot be transferred to it.

NVLink 6 scale-up bandwidth is a device-fabric aggregate across a GPU's NVLink links to the NVLink Switch; ConnectX-9 scale-out bandwidth is a network-port rate on a different interface, path and protocol, with its own counting. Converting 1.6 Tb/s to 200 GB/s puts both numbers in one unit but does not make them the same physical metric. As arithmetic only, the advertised 3.6 TB/s (stated bidirectional) is about 18 times 200 GB/s, or about 9 times 400 GB/s if 1.6 Tb/s is per direction; neither ratio describes relative delivered throughput.

pathway_divergence.justification: The pathway treats the pair as comparable after converting bits to bytes. A unit conversion makes the magnitudes expressible together but cannot make a device-fabric aggregate and a scale-out port rate the same metric; under this dossier's rules the two sit at different hierarchy levels.

cases.title: AMD MI300X Infinity Fabric
cases.question: What does AMD's 896 GB/s figure describe, and how does it relate to the 128 GB/s links?
established: AMD states the direction: 896 GB/s is a peak aggregate bidirectional figure, and each link is 128 GB/s bidirectional (IDE-009)
AMD lists seven 128 GB/s links per GPU and calls the platform eight GPUs in a ring with full connectivity
analysis: Seven links at 128 GB/s sum to exactly 896 GB/s; a platform-wide sum of the 28 links in a fully connected eight-GPU system would be 3,584 GB/s

The arithmetic is consistent with a per-GPU reading, but AMD's retrieved documents label the figure a ring-of-8 aggregate and never call it per GPU; arithmetic consistency is not a documentary statement
AMD's CDNA 4 paper uses the same '(8 GPUs)' label for a later figure it calls per GPU; a labelling convention in a later document does not state the scope of the MI300X figure
preserved: Direction is AMD-stated and is not reopened
The 2025 CDNA 4 edition with endnote MI350-007 is pending version verification and is not used as evidence

cases.title: NVIDIA Rubin HBM bandwidth
cases.question: What do NVIDIA's 22 TB/s and 19.2 TB/s figures for one Rubin GPU describe?
established: NVIDIA gives 22 TB/s in posts dated 2026-01-05 and 2026-07-21 and on its HGX page, and 19.2 TB/s in a post dated 2026-11-05 and on its Vera Rubin NVL72 page
Every source gives 288 GB of HBM4 per GPU; none withdraws either bandwidth figure
analysis: On NVIDIA's product pages the split follows the platform (HGX 22 TB/s, Vera Rubin NVL72 19.2 TB/s), and in its dated posts it follows the date (January and July 22 TB/s, November 19.2 TB/s); whether either pattern reflects different configurations is not stated

The HGX NVL8 row's 130 TB/s is 16.25 TB/s per GPU on even division, matching neither figure, so the row's bandwidth is not eight times either per-GPU figure. Its 2 TB of HBM4 also differs from eight times 288 GB (2,304 GB); the published figures do not explain whether rounding, a different configuration or another counting convention accounts for that
preserved: No explanation (product revision, preliminary figure, operating condition) is offered without a primary source

cases.title: NVLink 6 bandwidth
cases.question: What do NVIDIA's 3.6 TB/s and 3 TB/s NVLink 6 figures per Rubin GPU describe?
established: NVIDIA gives 3.6 TB/s (January post, marked bidirectional; HGX individual-GPU row) and 3,600 GB/s (July post), and 3 TB/s (November post; NVL72 GPU column)
Only the January post states a direction for a per-GPU figure
analysis: Every Rubin NVLink system aggregate reviewed divides evenly to 3 TB/s per GPU: 216 TB/s over 72 GPUs, and 24 TB/s (marked bidirectional) over 8 GPUs; 6 TB/s per superchip is consistent with 3 TB/s if a superchip has two GPUs
No reviewed aggregate divides to 3.6 TB/s; this shows NVIDIA's aggregates are consistent with each other, not which per-GPU figure is correct or what the 0.6 TB/s difference counts
Fabric bandwidth is kept apart from local memory bandwidth and from any measured collective throughput, none of which is published
preserved: The difference is not explained by assuming a direction convention for 3 TB/s

review_questions.question: In AMD's MI300X documentation, does 'P2P ring peak aggregate' bandwidth (896 GB/s) describe one GPU's seven links or a platform-level quantity?
review_questions.why_it_matters: It decides whether the figure can sit beside any per-GPU fabric figure.
review_questions.would_settle: An AMD statement of the figure's scope, or a version-identified copy of the 2025 CDNA 4 edition with endnote MI350-007

review_questions.question: Do NVIDIA's 22 TB/s and 19.2 TB/s per-GPU memory figures describe different Rubin configurations, and if so which?
review_questions.why_it_matters: Every per-GPU Rubin memory comparison depends on which figure applies to which product.
review_questions.would_settle: An NVIDIA specification that ties each figure to a configuration or memory operating point

review_questions.question: What counting convention gives 3.6 TB/s and what gives 3 TB/s per Rubin GPU for NVLink 6, given that NVIDIA's system aggregates divide evenly to 3 TB/s?
review_questions.why_it_matters: Scale-up comparisons and rack-to-GPU conversions depend on one consistent convention.
review_questions.would_settle: An NVIDIA statement of direction and counting for both figures

review_questions.question: For the x16 PCIe Gen 6 and CXL 3.0 figures of 256 GB/s, what share remains after encoding, FEC and protocol overhead?
review_questions.why_it_matters: Raw link figures are often compared with delivered throughput; the overhead decides how far they differ.
review_questions.would_settle: The normative PCIe 6.0 and CXL 3.x specifications, or a published measurement with its method

review_questions.question: Which published, reproducible measurements of collective bandwidth exist for the MI300X eight-GPU platform or Vera Rubin NVL72, and with what methods?
review_questions.why_it_matters: No figure in the dossier is measured; measured throughput is the evidence most comparisons actually need.
review_questions.would_settle: A measurement with workload, message sizes, software versions and topology stated

applications: Checking a draft comparison of accelerator bandwidth figures against the classification rules before it is published
Tracing any figure in this dossier to its publisher, date, exact passage and latest inspection
Converting rack or system aggregates to per-device values only where the rules allow, with the assumption stated
Listing the documents to request from a vendor before a bandwidth comparison can be defended (IDE-010 workflow B)
Giving a specialist a single, bounded question to review against public material

principal_findings.text: NVIDIA's Rubin NVLink system aggregates (216 TB/s over 72 GPUs, 24 TB/s over 8) divide evenly to 3 TB/s per GPU, never to 3.6 TB/s. This is an arithmetic consistency check, not an explanation of the difference.

NVIDIA's eight-GPU HGX memory figure (130 TB/s) divides to 16.25 TB/s, matching neither per-GPU memory figure. Its 2 TB capacity also differs from eight times 288 GB (2,304 GB), and the page does not say whether rounding, configuration or counting explains it.

AMD's 896 GB/s equals seven 128 GB/s links exactly, but AMD labels it a ring-of-8 aggregate and never calls it per GPU; arithmetic agreement does not settle its scope, so any comparison that relies on a per-GPU reading is indeterminate.
Halving a figure to a per-direction value is permitted only where the source states the direction; for NVLink 6 that is the January 3.6 TB/s figure alone.

public_reference_decision.reason: The /interconnects/ reference already presents each figure with its date and source, the 24 TB/s even-division arithmetic and the open conflicts. The dossier's additions (the classification method, rule-checked normalizations and cross-figure consistency) are unreviewed research and are kept out of the public reference until reviewed.
